name: Endoscopic foreheadplasty

lead: Endoscopic foreheadplasty lifts the eyebrows and forehead tissue through a few small incisions placed behind the hairline, with an endoscope (a thin camera) letting the surgeon see under the skin. The aim is to raise drooping or low brows, soften horizontal and frown lines and open the eye area, which can make the upper face look more rested and younger.

It was introduced to plastic surgery in the early 1990s as an alternative to the long scalp incision of the older coronal lift, and became a widely accepted procedure. Published work includes technique papers, a randomised comparison of dissection planes and reviews of complications.

paras: Patients consult a surgeon who assesses brow position, hairline height and skin thickness. The operation uses several short incisions at or behind the hairline; the forehead soft tissue is freed and repositioned and fixed with sutures, screws, staples or absorbable devices depending on the technique. It is often combined with eyelid surgery or a facelift. Swelling and bruising settle over days to weeks.

Reported complications include temporary weakness of forehead muscles or numbness, hair loss near incisions, asymmetry, a raised hairline, infection and bleeding; rare severe problems include motor nerve paresis and diplopia, usually temporary. Reviews note that no brow-lift technique is fully satisfactory because of limited effectiveness, longevity and complications. It is an operation for a board-certified surgeon to assess.

angle.text: The operation moves the brows to a higher position and smooths forehead lines, which changes how open and alert the eye area looks. Patients often combine it with eyelid surgery.

lead: Endoscopic foreheadplasty, also called the endoscopic forehead lift or endoscopic brow lift, is a cosmetic and reconstructive operation that raises the eyebrows and smooths the forehead using an endoscope inserted through small incisions behind the hairline [1][2]. It reshapes the upper third of the face: lifting heavy or low brows, softening horizontal forehead lines and the frown lines between the eyebrows, and opening the eye area.

In appearance-focused communities it is categorised as hard-maxxing, the surgical end of improvement, because it changes brow position and upper-face expression. The goal described by surgeons is a brow in a youthful, alert position [3]. A recent paper describes a customised endoscopic lift for men, reflecting differences in male brow shape [4].

Endoscopic techniques entered plastic surgery in the early 1990s, and the forehead lift was among the applications that gained general acceptance [5]. Reviews describe it as a less invasive alternative to the coronal lift, with the trade-offs noted below [6][7].

paras: Wikipedia describes endoscopic brow lifts as using thin, pencil-sized instruments through three to five small incisions, one carrying a camera whose view is shown on a monitor and guides the other instruments [8]. The procedure elevates drooping brows that can crowd the upper eyelids and reduces deep forehead lines [8]. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons describes a brow lift as smoothing forehead wrinkles, softening frown lines and placing the eyebrows in a youthful position, often combined with eyelid surgery or a facelift [9].

Technical papers describe variations: a subperiosteal approach with three small triangular prehairline incisions and release of periosteum at the supraorbital rims [2], and a subgaleal approach that resects muscle insertions with fixation by screws or staples that are removed after a week [10]. A randomised, self-controlled study compared subperiosteal and subgaleal elevation to find the best method for an aesthetically acceptable elevation [11]. Fixation devices such as a biodegradable implant (Endotine) were introduced to hold the lifted tissue [12].

The first documented medical discussion of a forehead lift was written in 1910 by the German surgeon Erich Lexer [8]. Endoscopic methods appeared in plastic surgery in the early 1990s, and the endoscopic forehead lift was accepted across a broad range of practices by the late 1990s [5]. Early endoscopic work extended to the full face; a 1994 paper introduced total subperiosteal dissection from the forehead down to the midface for patients up to their late 40s [13]. Surgeons published their preferences and technique summaries through the 1990s and 2000s [10][14].

Because forehead lifts can move the hairline, surgeons have written on how to avoid worsening a high forehead; one paper on hairline lowering notes that elevation occurs in both coronal and endoscopic techniques and that many patients with high hairlines worry about it [15]. A review of forehead lift for Asians notes anatomic differences, that endoscopic lift without a visible scar is favoured, and that a forehead lift may be considered before eyelid or nose surgery [3].

A review of the technique, cases and complications describes it as a minimally invasive alternative that avoids many undesirable effects of the coronal approach [2]. Wikipedia reports hair loss as most common after endoscopic lifts, infection and bleeding as general surgical risks, about 1% conversion to an open procedure, and that implants may shift during healing [8]. The review on Asian patients lists rare but severe complications such as motor nerve paresis and diplopia, which are temporary in most cases [3]. Anatomical studies of the supraorbital nerve show its exit point varies, which matters for dissection [16]. A narrative review of eyebrow-lifting techniques concluded that none are completely satisfactory because of limited effectiveness, lack of longevity and potential complications [6].

A randomised, self-controlled study compared three dissection techniques (subperiosteal, subperiosteal with periosteal release and subgaleal) for brow and forehead elevation and tension [11]. A case series of over 100 endoscopic forehead lifts described a technique with subgaleal muscle resection, periosteal release and vertical suspension [10]. A histologic study compared periosteal refixation after endoscopic and bicoronal lifts [17], and a study objectively assessed change in apparent age after facial rejuvenation surgery [18]. A 2025 paper reports a customised endoscopic male forehead/eyebrow lift [4].

timeline.event: Erich Lexer writes the first documented discussion of a forehead lift [8].
Endoscopic total subperiosteal facelift technique is described, extending the forehead lift concept to the midface [13].
A technique paper based on over 100 endoscopic forehead lifts is published [10].
A review notes the endoscopic forehead lift has general acceptance in plastic surgery practice [5].
A biodegradable fixation device (the Endotine) is described for endoscopic forehead lifts [12].
